title: The EU AI Act
hook: The EU's answer to regulating AI: sort systems by how much risk they pose, then scale the rules to match — from outright bans to no rules at all.
key_points: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 — described as the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide.
Takes a risk-based approach with four tiers: unacceptable (banned), high-risk, limited risk, and minimal risk.
Entered into force on 1 August 2024, with provisions phased in over time.
Bans on prohibited practices apply from February 2025; most rules from August 2026.
content_html: The EU AI Act — officially Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 — is described by the European Commission as the first-ever comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide. It sorts AI systems by how much risk they pose and scales obligations to match. This is a reference card; for the authoritative text and updates, follow the link out to the Commission's official page.
extra_html:
What it covers

The Act uses a risk-based approach with four tiers. Systems posing unacceptable risk are prohibited outright. High-risk systems carry strict obligations. Systems of transparency or limited risk face disclosure duties — users should know when they're dealing with AI. Systems of minimal or no risk get no specific rules. The framework entered into force on 1 August 2024 and phases in over time: bans on prohibited practices apply from February 2025, and most remaining rules from August 2026.

Why it matters

As the first comprehensive AI law, the EU AI Act sets a template other jurisdictions look to. Its tiered design means the heaviest requirements land on the riskiest uses while light-touch applications stay largely unburdened — a structure that shapes how companies building or deploying AI in Europe plan their compliance.
